## Introduction & Setup

This report investigates the spatial distribution and determinants of AirBnb property prices in Madrid, Spain, addressing the research tasks set out at the end of **Chapter 4** (*Point Data Analysis*), **Chapter 5** (*Spatial Interaction & Predictive Checking*), and **Chapter 6** (*Spatial Econometrics*).

### Required Libraries

We begin by loading the required spatial analysis, interpolation, econometric, and visualisation libraries in R.

```{r setup_packages}
# Data manipulation and transformation
library(tidyverse)
library(stringr)

# Spatial data handling and interpolation
library(sf)
library(sp)
library(gstat)
library(hexbin)

# Spatial weights and spatial econometrics
library(spdep)
library(spatialreg)

# Simulation and model diagnostics
library(arm)

# Visualisation, mapping, and tables
library(ggplot2)
library(gridExtra)
library(tmap)
library(viridis)
library(RColorBrewer)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
# Skip kableExtra's kePrint.js: it needs jQuery, which Quarto pages don't load
# ("$ is not defined"). The tables only use Bootstrap classes, so nothing is lost.
options(kableExtra.knit_print.dependency = FALSE)

# Disable spherical geometry (s2) for planar grid/interpolation compatibility
sf::sf_use_s2(FALSE)
set.seed(453)
```

### Madrid AirBnb Dataset

We load the pre-processed Madrid AirBnb GeoPackage (`madrid_abb.gpkg`) from `data/data_r/se_m_airbnb/assignment_1_madrid/` [@lovelace2019; @bivand2013].

```{r load_data}
# Robust relative path detection across development environments
data_candidates <- c(
  file.path("..", "..", "..", "data", "data_r", "se_m_airbnb", "assignment_1_madrid", "madrid_abb.gpkg"),
  file.path("data", "data_r", "se_m_airbnb", "assignment_1_madrid", "madrid_abb.gpkg")
)

data_path <- data_candidates[file.exists(data_candidates)][1]
mad_abb <- st_read(data_path, quiet = TRUE)
```

Let us inspect the available attributes, coordinate reference system (CRS), and summary statistics of the dataset.

```{r inspect_data}
colnames(mad_abb)
st_crs(mad_abb)$input
```

The dataset contains **`r nrow(mad_abb)`** AirBnb listings across **`r length(unique(mad_abb$neighbourhood))`** neighbourhoods in Madrid, stored as point geometries in WGS 84 (`EPSG:4326`). Key variables used across this assignment include:

- `price_usd`: Nightly listing price in USD ($P_i$).
- `log1p_price_usd`: Log-transformed nightly price, $\log(1 + P_i)$.
- `accommodates`: Guest capacity of the property ($Acc_i$).
- `bathrooms`: Number of bathrooms ($Bath_i$).
- `bedrooms`: Number of bedrooms ($Bedr_i$).
- `beds`: Number of beds ($Beds_i$).
- `neighbourhood`: Neighbourhood name ($r$) within Madrid.
- `km_to_retiro`: Euclidean distance (km) from the property to El Retiro Park.
- `WiFi`, `Coffee`, `Gym`, `Parking`: Binary amenity indicators (`1` = present, `0` = absent).
- `geom`: Point geometry ($X$ longitude, $Y$ latitude).

```{r summary_table}
desc_stats <- mad_abb %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  dplyr::select(price_usd, log1p_price_usd, accommodates, bathrooms, bedrooms, beds, km_to_retiro) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Variable", values_to = "Value") %>%
  group_by(Variable) %>%
  summarise(
    N = n(),
    Mean = round(mean(Value, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    SD = round(sd(Value, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    Min = round(min(Value, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    Median = round(median(Value, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    IQR = round(IQR(Value, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    Max = round(max(Value, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

kable(
  desc_stats,
  caption = "Table 1.1: Descriptive Statistics of Key Madrid AirBnb Variables"
) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"), full_width = FALSE)
```

## Point Data Analysis (Chapter 4 Tasks)

Chapter 4 focuses on visualising dense spatial point patterns and interpolating continuous attribute surfaces from point samples [@comber2015].

### Exploratory Price Distribution & Spatial Binning

Before constructing the spatial Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) and Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW) surfaces, we examine the non-spatial distribution of raw (`price_usd`) versus log-transformed (`log1p_price_usd`) prices, alongside 2D spatial binning of listing coordinates.

```{r fig_nonspatial_kde, fig.width=10, fig.height=4.5, fig.cap="Figure 1.1: Distribution and 1D KDE of Raw USD Prices (left) vs. Log-Transformed Prices (right) in Madrid."}
# Histogram + 1D KDE of raw price_usd
p_raw_hist <- ggplot(mad_abb, aes(x = price_usd)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, aes(y = after_stat(density)), fill = "grey35", colour = "white") +
  geom_density(fill = "#FF6666", alpha = 0.45, colour = "#FF6666", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(
    title = "Raw AirBnb Price (USD)",
    x = "Price (USD)",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# Histogram + 1D KDE of log1p_price_usd
p_log_hist <- ggplot(mad_abb, aes(x = log1p_price_usd)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, aes(y = after_stat(density)), fill = "grey35", colour = "white") +
  geom_density(fill = "#FF6666", alpha = 0.45, colour = "#FF6666", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(
    title = "Log-Transformed AirBnb Price",
    x = "log(1 + Price USD)",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

grid.arrange(p_raw_hist, p_log_hist, ncol = 2)
```

Raw AirBnb prices are heavily right-skewed (mean = \$`r round(mean(mad_abb$price_usd), 2)`, median = \$`r round(median(mad_abb$price_usd), 2)`, maximum = \$`r round(max(mad_abb$price_usd), 2)`), with most properties clustered below \$150 per night and a thin tail of luxury listings. Taking the natural logarithm (`log1p_price_usd`) compresses extreme values and yields a near-symmetric, bell-shaped distribution centered around `r round(mean(mad_abb$log1p_price_usd), 2)`.

To address point overplotting across the `r nrow(mad_abb)` locations, we first compare raw point plotting with two-dimensional square binning (`geom_bin2d`) and hexagonal binning (`geom_hex`).

```{r fig_binning, fig.width=11, fig.height=4.5, fig.cap="Figure 1.2: Spatial Distribution of Madrid AirBnb Listings using Square Binning (left) and Hexagonal Binning (right)."}
mad_coords <- as.data.frame(st_coordinates(mad_abb))

# Square 2D binning
sqbin <- ggplot() +
  geom_bin2d(data = mad_coords, aes(x = X, y = Y), bins = 40) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "viridis", name = "Count") +
  labs(title = "2D Square Binning", x = "Longitude (X)", y = "Latitude (Y)") +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_minimal()

# Hexagonal 2D binning
hexbin_plot <- ggplot() +
  geom_hex(data = mad_coords, aes(x = X, y = Y), bins = 40) +
  scale_fill_continuous(type = "viridis", name = "Count") +
  labs(title = "2D Hexagonal Binning", x = "Longitude (X)", y = "Latitude (Y)") +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_minimal()

grid.arrange(sqbin, hexbin_plot, ncol = 2)
```

### Task 4.1: Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) of AirBnb Locations in Madrid

To obtain a smooth, continuous surface representing the spatial intensity (probability density) of AirBnb property locations across Madrid, we apply two-dimensional Kernel Density Estimation (`stat_density2d_filled`).

```{r fig_spatial_kde, fig.width=9, fig.height=7, fig.cap="Figure 1.3: Two-Dimensional Spatial Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) of AirBnb Property Locations in Madrid."}
kde_surface <- ggplot(data = mad_abb) +
  stat_density2d_filled(
    data = mad_coords,
    aes(x = X, y = Y),
    alpha = 0.85,
    n = 100
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "viridis", name = "Density Level") +
  geom_sf(alpha = 0) +
  labs(
    title = "Spatial Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) of AirBnb Locations in Madrid",
    subtitle = "Continuous probability surface of listing concentration (WGS 84)",
    x = "Longitude",
    y = "Latitude"
  ) +
  theme_bw()

kde_surface
```

**Interpretation of the KDE Surface:**
The spatial KDE reveals an intense, monocentric concentration of AirBnb properties in the historic and tourist core of Madrid (`Centro` district, around longitudes $-3.71^\circ$ to $-3.69^\circ$ and latitudes $40.41^\circ$ to $40.43^\circ$, covering neighbourhoods such as *Sol*, *Embajadores*, *Palacio*, *Cortes*, *Justicia*, and *Universidad*). Density decays radially outward into surrounding residential districts (*Chamberí*, *Salamanca*, *Arganzuela*, *Retiro*, and *Tetuán*), with peripheral suburban districts exhibiting very sparse listing density.

### Task 4.2: Spatial Interpolation of AirBnb Prices via Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW)

While KDE estimates the density of *point occurrences*, it does not show how property *values* vary across space. To construct a continuous surface of AirBnb prices ($\hat{z}(x) = \sum_i w_i z_i / \sum_i w_i$), we apply Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW) interpolation [@comber2015; @cressie2015statistics]:

1. **Create a regular target grid (`mad.grid`)**: A $100 \times 100$ grid (10,000 evenly spaced prediction centres) spanning the bounding box of `mad_abb`.
2. **Compute IDW predictions**: Use `gstat::idw()` with `nmax = 150` nearest neighbours for both raw USD prices (`price_usd ~ 1`) and log-transformed prices (`log1p_price_usd ~ 1`).
3. **Render the interpolated raster surfaces**: Map the predicted values (`var1.pred`) across the grid.

```{r idw_grid_and_interpolation, results='hide'}
# 1. Create a 100 x 100 regular grid of cell centres over Madrid
mad.grid <- mad_abb %>%
  st_bbox() %>%
  st_as_sfc() %>%
  st_make_grid(
    n = 100,
    what = "centers"
  ) %>%
  st_as_sf() %>%
  cbind(., st_coordinates(.))

# Ensure identical CRS between source locations and target grid
st_crs(mad.grid) <- st_crs(mad_abb)

# 2. Fit IDW for raw price_usd (nmax = 150 nearest neighbours)
idw.raw <- idw(
  price_usd ~ 1,
  locations = mad_abb,
  newdata = mad.grid,
  nmax = 150
) %>%
  cbind(st_coordinates(.))

# 3. Fit IDW for log1p_price_usd (nmax = 150 nearest neighbours)
idw.log <- idw(
  log1p_price_usd ~ 1,
  locations = mad_abb,
  newdata = mad.grid,
  nmax = 150
) %>%
  cbind(st_coordinates(.))
```

Let us inspect the first rows of the interpolated IDW spatial object and plot both the raw price surface and the log-price surface.

```{r idw_head}
head(st_drop_geometry(idw.raw), 5)
```

```{r fig_idw_surface, fig.width=11, fig.height=5.5, fig.cap="Figure 1.4: Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW) Interpolated Surfaces of Madrid AirBnb Prices: Raw USD Price (left) and Log Price (right), using nmax = 150."}
p_idw_raw <- ggplot(idw.raw, aes(x = X, y = Y, fill = var1.pred)) +
  geom_raster() +
  scale_fill_viridis_b(option = "viridis", name = "Pred. USD ($)") +
  theme_void() +
  geom_sf(alpha = 0) +
  labs(
    title = "IDW Surface: Raw Price (USD)",
    subtitle = "Binned Viridis scale (nmax = 150)"
  ) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5))

p_idw_log <- ggplot(idw.log, aes(x = X, y = Y, fill = var1.pred)) +
  geom_raster() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma", name = "Pred. log(Price)") +
  theme_void() +
  geom_sf(alpha = 0) +
  labs(
    title = "IDW Surface: Log Price",
    subtitle = "Continuous Magma scale (nmax = 150)"
  ) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5))

grid.arrange(p_idw_raw, p_idw_log, ncol = 2)
```

We can also use the IDW model to predict the nightly price of a single hypothetical property located near El Retiro Park (`X = -3.6830, Y = 40.4153`):

```{r idw_single_point, results='hide'}
pt_retiro <- c(X = -3.6830, Y = 40.4153) %>%
  st_point() %>%
  st_sfc(crs = st_crs(mad_abb)) %>%
  st_sf()

idw.one <- idw(price_usd ~ 1, locations = mad_abb, newdata = pt_retiro, nmax = 150)
```

```{r idw_single_point_out}
cat("Predicted nightly price near El Retiro Park: $", round(idw.one$var1.pred[1], 2), "USD\n")
```

**Interpretation of the IDW Price Surface:**
Unlike the KDE map—where intensity peaks strictly in the historic center—the IDW price surface highlights distinct high-price corridors extending into affluent districts such as *Salamanca*, *Chamberí*, *Chamartín* (north-central Madrid), and the eastern perimeter near *San Blas-Canillejas* (around the Wanda Metropolitano stadium and IFEMA exhibition centre), while southern districts (*Usera*, *Villaverde*, *Puente de Vallecas*, *Carabanchel*) form a persistent low-price belt.

## Regression Modelling & Predictive Checks (Chapter 5 Tasks)

Chapter 5 focuses on building regression models of property prices and evaluating their adequacy through **Predictive Performance Checks (PPC)** that account for both point predictions and inferential/predictive simulation uncertainty [@gelman2006data].

### Task 5.1: Baseline Linear Regression Model for Raw Price ($P_i$)

We first estimate the baseline Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) model explaining raw price in USD (`price_usd`) as a linear function of four core structural property characteristics:

$$
P_i = \alpha + \beta_1 Acc_i + \beta_2 Bath_i + \beta_3 Bedr_i + \beta_4 Beds_i + \epsilon_i
$$

```{r model_ba_price}
ba.price <- lm(price_usd ~ accommodates + bathrooms + bedrooms + beds, data = mad_abb)
summary(ba.price)
```

### Task 5.2: Parallel Linear Regression Model for Log Price ($\log(P_i)$)

Next, we estimate a parallel OLS specification using the log-transformed price (`log1p_price_usd`) as the dependent variable:

$$
\log(P_i) = \alpha + \beta_1 Acc_i + \beta_2 Bath_i + \beta_3 Bedr_i + \beta_4 Beds_i + \epsilon_i
$$

```{r model_ba_log_price}
ba.log_price <- lm(log1p_price_usd ~ accommodates + bathrooms + bedrooms + beds, data = mad_abb)
summary(ba.log_price)
```

Let us compare the parameter estimates and fit statistics of both models in a formatted table.

```{r table_ch5_models}
ch5_comp <- tibble(
  Term = c("(Intercept)", "accommodates", "bathrooms", "bedrooms", "beds", "R-squared", "Adj. R-squared", "Residual SE"),
  `Model 1: Raw Price (USD)` = c(
    sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)***", coef(ba.price)[1], summary(ba.price)$coefficients[1, 2]),
    sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)***", coef(ba.price)[2], summary(ba.price)$coefficients[2, 2]),
    sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)***", coef(ba.price)[3], summary(ba.price)$coefficients[3, 2]),
    sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)***", coef(ba.price)[4], summary(ba.price)$coefficients[4, 2]),
    sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)***", coef(ba.price)[5], summary(ba.price)$coefficients[5, 2]),
    sprintf("%.4f", summary(ba.price)$r.squared),
    sprintf("%.4f", summary(ba.price)$adj.r.squared),
    sprintf("%.2f", summary(ba.price)$sigma)
  ),
  `Model 2: Log Price` = c(
    sprintf("%.4f (%.4f)***", coef(ba.log_price)[1], summary(ba.log_price)$coefficients[1, 2]),
    sprintf("%.4f (%.4f)***", coef(ba.log_price)[2], summary(ba.log_price)$coefficients[2, 2]),
    sprintf("%.4f (%.4f)***", coef(ba.log_price)[3], summary(ba.log_price)$coefficients[3, 2]),
    sprintf("%.4f (%.4f)***", coef(ba.log_price)[4], summary(ba.log_price)$coefficients[4, 2]),
    sprintf("%.4f (%.4f)***", coef(ba.log_price)[5], summary(ba.log_price)$coefficients[5, 2]),
    sprintf("%.4f", summary(ba.log_price)$r.squared),
    sprintf("%.4f", summary(ba.log_price)$adj.r.squared),
    sprintf("%.4f", summary(ba.log_price)$sigma)
  )
)

kable(
  ch5_comp,
  caption = "Table 2.1: Comparison of Baseline OLS Models for Raw Price (USD) vs. Log-Transformed Price (Standard Errors in Parentheses; *** p < 0.001)"
) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"), full_width = FALSE)
```

### Task 5.3: Predictive Check Analysis & Model Comparison

To evaluate how well each model captures the true data-generating process, we perform two levels of **Predictive Performance Checks (PPC)** following @gelman2006data:

1. **Point-Estimate Predictive Check**: Comparing the empirical kernel density of the deterministic fitted values ($\hat{y}_i = X_i\hat{\beta}$) against the observed outcome distribution ($y_i$).
2. **Simulated Predictive Check (Inferential + Predictive Uncertainty)**: Using `arm::sim()` to draw posterior parameter realisations ($\tilde{\beta}, \tilde{\sigma}$) and simulating 250 synthetic outcome vectors $\tilde{y} \sim \mathcal{N}(X\tilde{\beta}, \tilde{\sigma}^2)$.

```{r fig_ppc_point, fig.width=11, fig.height=5, fig.cap="Figure 2.1: Point-Estimate Predictive Checks: Fitted vs. Actual Density for the Raw Price Model (left) and Log-Price Model (right)."}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.2, 4.2, 3, 1))

# 1. Point-estimate check for Raw Price model
plot(
  density(ba.price$fitted.values),
  xlim = c(-50, 600),
  ylim = c(0, max(max(density(ba.price$fitted.values)$y), max(density(mad_abb$price_usd)$y)) * 1.05),
  col = "black",
  lwd = 2,
  xlab = "Price (USD)",
  ylab = "Density",
  main = "Point Check: Raw Price Model"
)
lines(density(mad_abb$price_usd), col = "red", lwd = 2)
legend("topright", legend = c("Predicted (Fitted)", "Actual"), col = c("black", "red"), lwd = 2, bty = "n")

# 2. Point-estimate check for Log Price model
plot(
  density(ba.log_price$fitted.values),
  xlim = c(1.5, 8.5),
  ylim = c(0, max(max(density(ba.log_price$fitted.values)$y), max(density(mad_abb$log1p_price_usd)$y)) * 1.05),
  col = "black",
  lwd = 2,
  xlab = "log(1 + Price USD)",
  ylab = "Density",
  main = "Point Check: Log Price Model"
)
lines(density(mad_abb$log1p_price_usd), col = "red", lwd = 2)
legend("topright", legend = c("Predicted (Fitted)", "Actual"), col = c("black", "red"), lwd = 2, bty = "n")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

Now we define the `generate_draw()` simulation function to incorporate both **inferential uncertainty** (uncertainty in $\hat{\beta}$) and **predictive uncertainty** (the error variance $\hat{\sigma}^2$), generating $n = 250$ simulated realisations for each model.

```{r fig_ppc_sim, fig.width=11, fig.height=5.2, fig.cap="Figure 2.2: Full Predictive Check with 250 Simulated Realisations (Grey) for the Raw Price Model (left) and Log-Price Model (right)."}
generate_draw <- function(m) {
  # Set up predictors matrix
  x <- model.matrix(m)
  # Obtain draws of parameters (inferential uncertainty)
  sim_bs <- sim(m, 1)
  # Predicted value
  mu <- x %*% sim_bs@coef[1, ]
  # Draw realization incorporating residual sigma (predictive uncertainty)
  n <- length(mu)
  y_hat <- rnorm(n, mu, sim_bs@sigma[1])
  return(y_hat)
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.2, 4.2, 3, 1))

# Left panel: Simulated PPC for Raw Price model
plot(
  density(ba.price$fitted.values),
  xlim = c(-300, 700),
  ylim = c(0, max(max(density(ba.price$fitted.values)$y), max(density(mad_abb$price_usd)$y)) * 1.05),
  col = "white",
  xlab = "Price (USD)",
  ylab = "Density",
  main = "Predictive Check (n=250): Raw Price"
)
for (i in 1:250) {
  tmp_y <- generate_draw(ba.price)
  lines(density(tmp_y), col = "grey75", lwd = 0.2)
}
lines(density(ba.price$fitted.values), col = "black", lwd = 2)
lines(density(mad_abb$price_usd), col = "red", lwd = 2)
abline(v = 0, lty = 2, col = "blue")
legend(
  "topright",
  legend = c("Actual", "Predicted", "Simulated (n=250)", "Zero Boundary"),
  col = c("red", "black", "grey60", "blue"),
  lwd = c(2, 2, 1, 1),
  lty = c(1, 1, 1, 2),
  bty = "n",
  cex = 0.85
)

# Right panel: Simulated PPC for Log Price model
plot(
  density(ba.log_price$fitted.values),
  xlim = c(1.5, 8.5),
  ylim = c(0, max(max(density(ba.log_price$fitted.values)$y), max(density(mad_abb$log1p_price_usd)$y)) * 1.05),
  col = "white",
  xlab = "log(1 + Price USD)",
  ylab = "Density",
  main = "Predictive Check (n=250): Log Price"
)
for (i in 1:250) {
  tmp_y <- generate_draw(ba.log_price)
  lines(density(tmp_y), col = "grey75", lwd = 0.2)
}
lines(density(ba.log_price$fitted.values), col = "black", lwd = 2)
lines(density(mad_abb$log1p_price_usd), col = "red", lwd = 2)
legend(
  "topright",
  legend = c("Actual", "Predicted", "Simulated (n=250)"),
  col = c("red", "black", "grey60"),
  lwd = c(2, 2, 1),
  bty = "n",
  cex = 0.85
)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

**Discussion and Model Selection:**

1. **Explanatory Power ($R^2$) and Coefficient Interpretation**:
   - In both models, `accommodates`, `bathrooms`, and `bedrooms` have statistically significant positive effects on price ($p < 0.001$), whereas `beds` has a statistically significant negative coefficient holding the other predictors constant. This negative partial effect of `beds` arises because, for a fixed number of bedrooms and guests (`bedrooms` and `accommodates` held constant), adding more beds indicates shared/crowded sleeping arrangements (e.g., hostels or subdivided rooms), which command lower nightly rates.
   - However, the **raw price model (`ba.price`)** explains only **`r round(summary(ba.price)$r.squared * 100, 1)`%** of the variance in price ($R^2 = `r round(summary(ba.price)$r.squared, 4)`$), with a massive residual standard error of **\$`r round(summary(ba.price)$sigma, 2)`**.
   - By contrast, the **log-price model (`ba.log_price`)** more than doubles the explained variance to **`r round(summary(ba.log_price)$r.squared * 100, 1)`%** ($R^2 = `r round(summary(ba.log_price)$r.squared, 4)`$). Its coefficients have a clean multiplicative (semi-elasticity) interpretation: each additional guest accommodated increases price by approximately **`r round(coef(ba.log_price)["accommodates"] * 100, 1)`%**, an additional bathroom increases price by **`r round(coef(ba.log_price)["bathrooms"] * 100, 1)`%**, an additional bedroom adds **`r round(coef(ba.log_price)["bedrooms"] * 100, 1)`%**, and an extra bed (holding capacity and bedrooms constant) reduces price by **`r abs(round(coef(ba.log_price)["beds"] * 100, 1))`%**.

2. **Predictive Check Comparison (Why the Log-Price Model is Preferred)**:
   - **Failure of the Raw Price Model**: Because `price_usd` has extreme positive outliers, the Gaussian error assumption $\epsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$ inflates $\hat{\sigma}$ to \$`r round(summary(ba.price)$sigma, 1)`. Consequently, the 250 simulated draws (Figure 2.2, left) form a flat, wide normal curve that completely misses the sharp empirical peak around \$50–\$80 and assigns substantial probability mass to **impossible negative prices** (left of the dashed blue line at \$0).
   - **Superiority of the Log-Price Model**: In the log-price specification (Figure 2.2, right), while the deterministic point estimates (black curve) are naturally narrower than the observed data (since $\text{Var}(\hat{y}) < \text{Var}(y)$), the 250 simulated draws (grey band) closely envelope the actual empirical distribution (red curve) in location, spread, and symmetry. Furthermore, exponentiating log-price predictions ($\hat{P}_i = \exp(\widehat{\log P_i}) - 1$) guarantees strictly positive price predictions. Therefore, the **log-price model (`ba.log_price`) is strongly preferred**.

## Spatial Econometrics: Heterogeneity & Dependence (Chapter 6 Tasks)

While the log-price model improves functional form, it treats observations as spatially independent and homogeneous across Madrid. In Chapter 6, we incorporate **spatial heterogeneity** (via neighbourhood fixed effects and spatial regimes) and **spatial dependence** (via spatial weight matrices and exogenous spatial lags) [@anselin1988spatial; @anselin2003spatial; @reyABwolf].

```{r fig_price_and_neighbourhood_map, fig.width=11, fig.height=5, fig.cap="Figure 3.1: Spatial Distribution of Log Prices (left) and Neighbourhood Administrative Groupings (right) across Madrid."}
p_map_price <- mad_abb %>%
  ggplot(aes(color = log1p_price_usd)) +
  geom_sf(size = 0.4, alpha = 0.75) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(option = "viridis", name = "log(1+Price)") +
  labs(title = "Spatial Distribution of Log AirBnb Prices") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"))

p_map_nei <- mad_abb %>%
  ggplot(aes(color = neighbourhood)) +
  geom_sf(size = 0.4, alpha = 0.75, show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(title = paste0("Madrid Neighbourhoods (n = ", length(unique(mad_abb$neighbourhood)), ")")) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"))

grid.arrange(p_map_price, p_map_nei, ncol = 2)
```

### Task 6.1: Baseline Non-Spatial Log-Price Model (`m1`)

We begin with the baseline non-spatial model explaining `log1p_price_usd` solely through structural property attributes:

$$
\log(P_i) = \alpha + \beta_1 Acc_i + \beta_2 Bath_i + \beta_3 Bedr_i + \beta_4 Beds_i + \epsilon_i
$$

```{r ch6_m1}
m1 <- lm(log1p_price_usd ~ accommodates + bathrooms + bedrooms + beds, data = mad_abb)
summary(m1)
```

**Interpretation (`m1`):**
All four structural predictors are highly statistically significant ($p < 0.001$), explaining **`r round(summary(m1)$r.squared * 100, 2)`%** of log-price variation. However, `m1` assumes a single global intercept ($\hat{\alpha} = `r round(coef(m1)[1], 3)`$) across all of Madrid, ignoring unobserved neighbourhood prestige, accessibility, and locational amenities, which become absorbed into the error term $\epsilon_i$.

### Task 6.2: Spatial Fixed Effects at the Neighbourhood Level (`m2`)

To account for **spatial heterogeneity** at the neighbourhood scale, we allow the intercept $\alpha_r$ to vary across each neighbourhood $r \in \{1, \dots, 128\}$ by introducing neighbourhood indicator variables without a global constant (`- 1`):

$$
\log(P_i) = \alpha_r + \beta_1 Acc_i + \beta_2 Bath_i + \beta_3 Bedr_i + \beta_4 Beds_i + \epsilon_i
$$

```{r ch6_m2}
m2 <- lm(
  log1p_price_usd ~ neighbourhood + accommodates + bathrooms + bedrooms + beds - 1,
  data = mad_abb
)

# Display the structural property coefficients from the Spatial FE model
round(tail(summary(m2)$coefficients, 4), 4)
cat("Spatial FE R-squared:", round(summary(m2)$r.squared, 4),
    "| Adjusted R-squared:", round(summary(m2)$adj.r.squared, 4), "\n")
```

We now extract the estimated neighbourhood fixed effects ($\hat{\alpha}_r$) and map them to visualise Madrid's **"Geography of Desirability"**.

```{r fig_spatial_fe_map, fig.width=10, fig.height=6, fig.cap="Figure 3.2: Geography of Desirability in Madrid: Estimated Neighbourhood Fixed Effects (alpha_r) from Model m2."}
# Extract neighbourhood fixed-effect coefficients
coef_df <- data.frame(
  term = names(m2$coefficients),
  coef = as.numeric(m2$coefficients),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
) %>%
  dplyr::filter(str_starts(term, "neighbourhood")) %>%
  mutate(nei = str_replace(term, "^neighbourhood", ""))

# Join fixed effects back to spatial points
nei.fes <- coef_df %>%
  right_join(mad_abb, by = c("nei" = "neighbourhood")) %>%
  st_as_sf()

# Plot the geography of desirability
ggplot(nei.fes, aes(color = coef)) +
  geom_sf(size = 0.6, alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(option = "viridis", name = expression(hat(alpha)[r])) +
  labs(
    title = "Geography of Desirability: Neighbourhood Fixed Effects in Madrid",
    subtitle = "Baseline log-price premium by neighbourhood controlling for property size"
  ) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5)
  )
```

**Interpretation (`m2`):**
Introducing neighbourhood fixed effects isolates *within-neighbourhood* variation, controlling for unobserved time-invariant spatial confounders (such as historic architecture, metro access, and prestige). The structural coefficients remain highly significant (`accommodates` = `r round(coef(m2)["accommodates"], 3)`, `bathrooms` = `r round(coef(m2)["bathrooms"], 3)`, `bedrooms` = `r round(coef(m2)["bedrooms"], 3)`, `beds` = `r round(coef(m2)["beds"], 3)`), and the mapped $\hat{\alpha}_r$ estimates (Figure 3.2) reveal a clear core-periphery and north-south gradient: central and wealthy northern neighbourhoods (*Recoletos*, *Castellana*, *Jerónimos*, *Sol*, *Goya*) command the highest baseline willingness-to-pay, whereas southern working-class neighbourhoods (*San Cristóbal*, *Amposta*, *Entrevías*, *Zofío*) have the lowest baseline intercepts.

### Task 6.3: Spatial Regimes at the Neighbourhood Level (`m3`)

Spatial fixed effects (`m2`) allow only the intercept ($\alpha_r$) to vary geographically while restricting the slope parameters ($\beta_1, \dots, \beta_4$) to be uniform across Madrid. **Spatial regimes (`m3`)** generalise spatial heterogeneity by allowing both the intercept and all structural slope coefficients to vary across neighbourhoods:

$$
\log(P_i) = \alpha_r + \beta_{r1} Acc_i + \beta_{r2} Bath_i + \beta_{r3} Bedr_i + \beta_{r4} Beds_i + \epsilon_{ri}
$$

```{r ch6_m3}
mad_abb$one <- 1

m3 <- lm(
  log1p_price_usd ~ 0 + (one + accommodates + bathrooms + bedrooms + beds):(neighbourhood),
  data = mad_abb
)

cat("Spatial Regimes R-squared:", round(summary(m3)$r.squared, 4),
    "| Adjusted R-squared:", round(summary(m3)$adj.r.squared, 4), "\n")
```

Let us compare the nested progression from `m1` (Pooled OLS) to `m2` (Spatial Fixed Effects) to `m3` (Spatial Regimes) using an $F$-test (`anova`) and visualise the distribution of neighbourhood-specific slope estimates $\hat{\beta}_{rk}$ across Madrid.

```{r anova_heterogeneity}
anova(m1, m2, m3)
```

```{r fig_spatial_regimes_slopes, fig.width=10, fig.height=4.5, fig.cap="Figure 3.3: Distribution of Neighbourhood-Specific Slope Estimates (Spatial Regimes Model m3) vs. Global Pooled OLS Estimates (Dashed Red Line)."}
sr_coefs <- tibble(
  term = names(coef(m3)),
  estimate = as.numeric(coef(m3))
) %>%
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(estimate)) %>%
  mutate(
    variable = case_when(
      str_starts(term, "accommodates:") ~ "accommodates",
      str_starts(term, "bathrooms:") ~ "bathrooms",
      str_starts(term, "bedrooms:") ~ "bedrooms",
      str_starts(term, "beds:") ~ "beds",
      TRUE ~ "intercept"
    )
  ) %>%
  dplyr::filter(variable != "intercept", abs(estimate) < 1.5)

global_refs <- tibble(
  variable = c("accommodates", "bathrooms", "bedrooms", "beds"),
  global_est = as.numeric(coef(m1)[c("accommodates", "bathrooms", "bedrooms", "beds")])
)

ggplot(sr_coefs, aes(x = estimate)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 35, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white", alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_vline(data = global_refs, aes(xintercept = global_est), colour = "red", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free", nrow = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Spatial Regimes (m3): Distribution of Local Slope Coefficients across Neighbourhoods",
    subtitle = "Red dashed line indicates the global baseline OLS estimate (m1)",
    x = "Estimated Coefficient (within Neighbourhood)",
    y = "Number of Neighbourhoods"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

**Interpretation (`m3`):**
Allowing slopes to vary by neighbourhood significantly reduces the residual sum of squares compared to both `m1` and `m2` ($p < 0.001$ in the `anova` $F$-test), raising the unadjusted $R^2$ from **`r round(summary(m1)$r.squared, 3)`** (`m1`) to **`r round(summary(m3)$r.squared, 3)`** (`m3`). This indicates that the marginal valuation of an extra bedroom or bathroom differs across sub-markets (e.g., central tourist apartments vs. suburban family homes). However, estimating 5 parameters across 128 neighbourhoods consumes over 600 degrees of freedom, causing some small neighbourhoods with few listings to exhibit noisy or unidentifiable (`NA`) slope estimates—a classic bias-variance trade-off in unrestricted spatial regime models.

### Task 6.4: Spatial Weights Matrix & Exogenous Spatial Lag Model (`m4` & `m5`)

Unlike spatial heterogeneity (which links outcomes to administrative areas), **spatial dependence** captures how observations interact directly across distance [@anselin2014modern; @gibbons2014spatial]. We construct a row-standardised $k$-nearest neighbours ($k = 50$) spatial weights matrix $W$, where $w_{ij} = 1/50$ if listing $j$ is among the 50 closest properties to listing $i$, and $w_{ij} = 0$ otherwise.

```{r build_knn_weights}
# Construct k = 50 nearest-neighbour spatial weights matrix
hnn <- mad_abb %>%
  st_coordinates() %>%
  as.matrix() %>%
  knearneigh(k = 50)

hnb <- knn2nb(hnn)
hknn <- nb2listw(hnb, style = "W")
hknn
```

First, we verify the presence of global spatial autocorrelation in `log1p_price_usd` and in the baseline OLS residuals (`m1`) using Moran's $I$.

```{r moran_tests}
moran_price <- moran.test(mad_abb$log1p_price_usd, hknn)
moran_res <- lm.morantest(m1, hknn)

cat("Moran's I on log1p_price_usd:", round(moran_price$estimate[1], 4),
    "(p-value:", format.pval(moran_price$p.value), ")\n")
cat("Moran's I on Baseline m1 Residuals:", round(moran_res$estimate[1], 4),
    "(p-value:", format.pval(moran_res$p.value), ")\n")
```

**Motivation for the Spatial Lag Variable(s):**
We motivate two complementary **Exogenous Spatial Lag (SLX)** models:

1. **Spatial Lag of Bathrooms (`w_bathrooms`, Model `m4`)**: Following the course framework in Chapter 6, the number of bathrooms in a property serves as a proxy for housing size, build quality, and luxury status. The spatial lag $W \cdot \text{Bath}_i = \sum_j w_{ij} \text{Bath}_j$ measures the average number of bathrooms among the 50 nearest surrounding AirBnb listings. If a property is surrounded by large, high-end apartments, positive neighbourhood status externalities and local market comparables should raise its nightly price even holding its own structural characteristics constant:
   $$
   \log(P_i) = \alpha + \beta_1 Acc_i + \beta_2 Bath_i + \beta_3 Bedr_i + \beta_4 Beds_i + \beta_5 Bath_{\text{lag}-i} + \epsilon_i
   $$
2. **Spatial Lag of Guest Capacity (`w_accommodates`) & Distance to El Retiro (`km_to_retiro`, Model `m5`)**: In Madrid, proximity to the city's premier green/cultural landmark (`km_to_retiro`) and the surrounding density of large tourist accommodations (`w_accommodates`) alongside `w_bathrooms` capture both local housing prestige and urban centrality externalities.

```{r ch6_slx_models}
# Compute spatial lags using W (k = 50 nearest neighbours)
mad_abb$w_bathrooms <- lag.listw(hknn, mad_abb$bathrooms)
mad_abb$w_accommodates <- lag.listw(hknn, mad_abb$accommodates)

# Model m4: Baseline + Spatial lag of bathrooms (w_bathrooms)
m4 <- lm(
  log1p_price_usd ~ accommodates + bedrooms + beds + bathrooms + w_bathrooms,
  data = mad_abb
)
summary(m4)

# Model m5: Extended spatial model adding w_accommodates and km_to_retiro
m5 <- lm(
  log1p_price_usd ~ accommodates + bedrooms + beds + bathrooms + w_bathrooms + w_accommodates + km_to_retiro,
  data = mad_abb
)
summary(m5)
```

Let us synthesise all Chapter 6 spatial econometric models in a comprehensive comparison table (`Table 3.1`) and demonstrate out-of-sample price prediction for a hypothetical Madrid property.

```{r table_ch6_summary}
model_summary_tbl <- tibble(
  Model = c(
    "m1: Baseline OLS",
    "m2: Neighbourhood Fixed Effects (FE)",
    "m3: Neighbourhood Spatial Regimes (SR)",
    "m4: SLX (Spatial Lag of Bathrooms)",
    "m5: Extended SLX (w_bathrooms + w_accommodates + km_to_retiro)"
  ),
  `Accommodates` = c(
    round(coef(m1)["accommodates"], 4),
    round(coef(m2)["accommodates"], 4),
    round(median(sr_coefs$estimate[sr_coefs$variable == "accommodates"], na.rm = TRUE), 4),
    round(coef(m4)["accommodates"], 4),
    round(coef(m5)["accommodates"], 4)
  ),
  `Bathrooms` = c(
    round(coef(m1)["bathrooms"], 4),
    round(coef(m2)["bathrooms"], 4),
    round(median(sr_coefs$estimate[sr_coefs$variable == "bathrooms"], na.rm = TRUE), 4),
    round(coef(m4)["bathrooms"], 4),
    round(coef(m5)["bathrooms"], 4)
  ),
  `Bedrooms` = c(
    round(coef(m1)["bedrooms"], 4),
    round(coef(m2)["bedrooms"], 4),
    round(median(sr_coefs$estimate[sr_coefs$variable == "bedrooms"], na.rm = TRUE), 4),
    round(coef(m4)["bedrooms"], 4),
    round(coef(m5)["bedrooms"], 4)
  ),
  `Beds` = c(
    round(coef(m1)["beds"], 4),
    round(coef(m2)["beds"], 4),
    round(median(sr_coefs$estimate[sr_coefs$variable == "beds"], na.rm = TRUE), 4),
    round(coef(m4)["beds"], 4),
    round(coef(m5)["beds"], 4)
  ),
  `w_bathrooms` = c(
    "—", "—", "—",
    as.character(round(coef(m4)["w_bathrooms"], 4)),
    as.character(round(coef(m5)["w_bathrooms"], 4))
  ),
  `Adj. R2` = c(
    round(summary(m1)$adj.r.squared, 4),
    round(summary(m2)$adj.r.squared, 4),
    round(summary(m3)$adj.r.squared, 4),
    round(summary(m4)$adj.r.squared, 4),
    round(summary(m5)$adj.r.squared, 4)
  ),
  AIC = c(
    round(AIC(m1), 1),
    round(AIC(m2), 1),
    round(AIC(m3), 1),
    round(AIC(m4), 1),
    round(AIC(m5), 1)
  )
)

kable(
  model_summary_tbl,
  caption = "Table 3.1: Comparative Summary of Spatial Econometric Specifications for Madrid AirBnb Log Prices (Note: m3 reports median regime slope)"
) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"), full_width = FALSE)
```

```{r predict_new_house}
# Predict price for a hypothetical property in Madrid using m4
new.house <- data.frame(
  accommodates = 4,
  bedrooms = 2,
  beds = 3,
  bathrooms = 1,
  w_bathrooms = 1.5
)

new.log.price <- predict(m4, new.house)
new.usd.price <- expm1(new.log.price)
cat("Predicted log1p(price):", round(new.log.price, 4),
    "| Predicted nightly price: $", round(new.usd.price, 2), "USD\n")
```

**Interpretation (`m4` & `m5`):**
In `m4`, the spatial lag of bathrooms (`w_bathrooms`) is positive (`r round(coef(m4)["w_bathrooms"], 4)`) and highly statistically significant ($p < 0.001$), and its magnitude is substantially larger than the property's own bathroom coefficient (`bathrooms` = `r round(coef(m4)["bathrooms"], 4)`). Econometrically, this demonstrates strong **exogenous spatial spillovers**: while a single apartment's bathroom count is noisy, the average bathroom count of the 50 surrounding listings acts as a robust local indicator of housing stock wealth and neighbourhood prestige. In `m5`, adding `w_accommodates` (`r round(coef(m5)["w_accommodates"], 4)`, $p < 0.001$) and distance to El Retiro Park (`km_to_retiro` = `r round(coef(m5)["km_to_retiro"], 4)`, $p < 0.001$, indicating an approximate `r abs(round(coef(m5)["km_to_retiro"] * 100, 1))`% price decay per kilometre away from El Retiro) further improves model fit (Adjusted $R^2 = `r round(summary(m5)$adj.r.squared, 4)`$, AIC = `r round(AIC(m5), 1)`), confirming that both local spatial context and urban centrality are critical determinants of AirBnb prices in Madrid.
